newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French government takes its time on EMU.
newsitem.headline: New French government takes its time on EMU.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government kept Europe waiting on Friday for a clear statement of its position on conditions for a single European currency.

On his first foreign outing since taking office, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin sidestepped the issue at a European Social Democrats' congress in Sweden, saying it was too early to take a stance on a stability pact limiting budget deficits of countries that join economic and monetary union (EMU).

Asked when France's position on the stability pact and the single currency would be announced, he told reporters in Malmo: "Days or weeks. Things are starting. We don't know when it will be achieved."

Jospin called for a more socially-minded Europe and said prospects for the single currency were "delicate", a view he shared with British Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair at a short meeting on Thursday night.
During the election campaign, Jospin branded the stability pact an "absurd" concession to Germany and a deviation from the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, and said he did not feel bound by it.

He also said the left would not inflict a further bout of austerity on France if it were necessary to meet the strict terms for launching the euro currency on time in 1999, saying the criteria should be interpreted more loosely.
Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said on May 2 the party wanted guarantees that member states would not be obliged to cut deficits below three percent of gross domestic product.

New Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn is due to meet EU colleagues in Luxembourg on Monday but his office said he would not attend an informal dinner on Sunday night, at which ministers had hoped to size up Paris' stance on EMU.
Time is pressing. EU leaders are due to approve the stability pact, negotiated in Dublin last December, at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

A spokesman for the EU's Dutch presidency said on Friday that France had not officially requested any reopening of the stability pact. Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo will meet the new French line-up in Paris on Tuesday to prepare for the Amsterdam conference.

Former European Commission president Jacques Delors, who has been acting as an informal spokesman for Jospin in an attempt to reassure European partners, told Friday's International Herald Tribune that France would take the necessary measures to launch the single currency on time in January 1999.
Asked about the risk of a delay, he said: "There's only one place where that will be decided, and that's in Germany."

Any change in the French position would have to be coordinated with conservative President Jacques Chirac under the "cohabitation" system of power-sharing forced by the left's upset parliamentary election victory.

The Socialist party set conditions for backing a single currency during the election campaign -- a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty, early membership for Italy and Spain, a European economic government, a new solidarity and growth pact and a euro which is not overvalued.
Chirac, who is due to meet both Blair and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl next week, said during the campaign that he would guarantee that France met its European commitments.

Greeted by delegates with a standing ovation on arrival at the European Social Democratic Parties' Congress, Jospin focused on the need to fight unemployment, encourage economic growth and foster equality among citizens of the European Union.

He said that his government would remain faithful to its election manifesto but later brushed off questions, saying: "I've just arrived (in office). I'm starting to go through the papers. I will not speak on questions of substance here today."
"On the stability pact, I have no comment," he said.
Jospin distanced himself from the federalism of some French Socialists, saying that while the ideal was to build a united Europe, the individual sovereign state was the building block.
"Europe cannot replace nations," he said. "Nation states remain the historic centre of democracy."
He welcomed Labour's landslide victory in the May 1 British elections and said that together with his own win it offered a chance to build a new Europe.
